alhaka reads what other teams built for the
[Alpaca AI Trading Agents Hackathon](https://lablab.ai/ai-hackathons/alpaca-ai-trading-agents-hackathon)
on lablab.ai and distills it into notes for building agentic trading prototypes. The field is
427 public submissions. Our own entry is
[PACA, the Position-aware Agentic Capital Allocator](https://lablab.ai/ai-hackathons/alpaca-ai-trading-agents-hackathon/win-or-die/paca-position-aware-agentic-capital-allocator);
everything else here is about learning from the other 426.

The repository is a monorepo in the making. The main branch holds the research tooling, the
generated research pages, and the posts that follow up on them. Trading code lives on other
branches: PACA on its own, and code borrowed from other submissions, modified and tested, on
branches of their own.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Start here

[What the other teams built](pages/hackathon-submissions.qmd) maps every submission to one
of 13 trading approaches, with a one-line notable idea per project.
:::

## What is here

- **[The category map](pages/hackathon-submissions.qmd).** All 427 projects, grouped by primary
  trading approach rather than asset class or tech stack, with category definitions, community
  vote counts and a notable idea for each. Generated, so it can be rebuilt when the field changes.
- **[Posts](posts.qmd).** Hand-written follow-up studies that ask one question of the field.
  The first, [Market-structure ideas in the hackathon field](posts/market-structure-submissions.qmd),
  looks for volume profile, order flow, dealer positioning and auction theory across the submissions.
- **[About](about.qmd).** Who is behind this.

## How the map was built

Submissions were pulled from lablab's public submissions API. Only each team's written summary,
the same text shown on its lablab page, was read; presentations, repositories and demos were not
opened. Projects were split into batches and read by parallel LLM subagents in two passes. The
first pass proposed categories from what each project's agents actually do, and those proposals
were merged by hand into a taxonomy. The second pass assigned every project to exactly one
category and wrote its notable line, grounded in the summary alone. A deterministic script then
merged the assignments and rendered the page, refusing to write if any project was missing,
duplicated or filed under an unknown category.

Three caveats apply throughout. Summaries are marketing copy capped at 2,000 characters, so a
project may do more or less than it claims. A project combining several approaches sits under its
primary one. Vote counts are community likes on lablab, not judging results.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Read the field

Start with the [category definitions](pages/hackathon-submissions.qmd#category-definitions),
then jump to the approach closest to what you are building.
:::
